Project Summary: Satellite Launcher
Satellite Launcher is an engaging, web-based interactive simulation game that empowers students and aspiring engineers to design, manage, and execute complete space missions from concept to operation.

To address the gap between abstract aerospace theories and real-world systems engineering, the game allows individual players or collaborative teams of up to four to define mission objectives, select scientific payloads, choose orbits and launch vehicles, and balance tight resource constraints including mass, power, budget, data volume, and lifespan. Every engineering trade-off directly impacts mission performance and success.

This project is important because it transforms complex aerospace concepts—such as orbital mechanics, payload compatibility, and resource budgeting—into an intuitive, hands-on learning experience. By simulating real-world decision-making cycles inspired by NASA frameworks like the Mission Design Lab, Satellite Launcher fosters critical thinking, collaborative negotiation, and a deep, practical understanding of modern space mission architecture.

Satellite Launcher

Satellite Launcher is a browser-based space arcade game that puts players in control of a rocket on a satellite deployment mission. Players must lift off from Earth, reach a target orbit, and deploy their satellite while managing the rocket’s fuel and integrity, steering around space debris, and aligning their trajectory.

The mission target is an altitude of 400 km and a velocity of 7.7 km/s. An on-screen mission display tracks altitude, velocity, score, stage, fuel reserve, rocket integrity, and orbital alignment. Players steer and thrust with the WASD keys or arrow keys, then deploy the satellite when the rocket reaches the target orbit. On mobile devices, they can use the on-screen controls.

The game is aimed at casual players and space enthusiasts looking for a short, interactive challenge. Its workflow is straightforward: initiate the launch, guide the rocket through the ascent, monitor mission conditions, and deploy the satellite once the target orbit is reached.
